messages.subject: Mixture of Gamma distributions
parts:
I have the following model:
lambda~gamma(1,1)
pi~Dirichlet([1,1]) #uniform prior
y~pi[1]*exponential(lambda[1])+pi[2]*exponential(lambda[2])

I am using the following stan file to do inference on a given dataset (which was generated where pi=[0.4, 0.6] and lambda=[2, 6] and N=50).

data {

        int<lower=1> N;

        int<lower=1> k;

        real<lower=0> y[N];

}

parameters {

        simplex[k] pi;

        real<lower=0> lambda[k];

}

model {

        real ps[k];

        for (i in 1:k){

                lambda[k] ~ gamma(1,1);

        }

        for (i in 1:N){

                for (j in 1:k){

                        ps[j]<-log(pi[j])+gamma_log(y[i],1,lambda[j]);

                }

                increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(ps));

        }

}


However, it is giving me the error 

"Exception thrown at line 17: gamma_log: Inverse scale parameter is 0, but must be > 0!        777

Exception thrown at line 17: gamma_log: Inverse scale parameter is inf, but must be finite!     1"


I'm guessing I've done the stan file wrong. Even when I extract the data and check it the lambda values are extremely large.


If it help I've attached the relevant R script and the data. 


Cheers,

Sachin

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Mixture of Gamma distributions
parts:
The Stan program looks OK to me as a mixture of
exponentials. I have no idea how easy such a model is
to fit.

Were the posterior inferences OK aside from the warnings?

And were you fitting simulated data? You want to do that
to verify everything's working and avoid the possiblity
of numerical issues due to model misspecification.

I'd also suggest using exponential_log(y[i], lambda)
instead of gamma_log(y[i], 1, 1/lambda). And
you can vectorize the lambda sampling statement.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: Mixture of Gamma distributions
parts:
Just incase anyone is interested I 'fixed' the problem by setting limits to lambda. In the parameters block I made the following change:

real<lower=min(y), upper=max(y)> lambda[k];


Note: I made a mistake in the above question. I should have said that y~pi[1]*exponential(1/lambda[1])+pi[2]*exponential(1/lambda[2]). This way the mean of y is lambda.


The reason for the above limit is that it is conceivable that the MEAN of y (lambda) is between the max and min of y.


@Bob apologies if this is trivial but how do you vectorise the lambda sampling statement. Is it simply:

lambda~exponential(1)
